paras: The lynching of Chubb McCarthy took place early on 28 June 1888, when a mob took McCarthy, accused of murdering Mike Dorsey, from the jail at Minneapolis, Kansas, and hanged him from a bridge over the Solomon River. The mob held the sheriff and city marshal under guard while it worked, and the body was found hanging at 7 a.m. Newspapers across the country reported it as the last of four lynchings in Kansas within twenty-four hours, which the wire report linked to the state's death-penalty law.

Mike Dorsey of Fountain Township, Ottawa County, was said to have been murdered in his bed at his home near Fountain a few days before the lynching, and McCarthy was charged with the killing. McCarthy was held in the Minneapolis jail "awaiting the action of the Grand Jury," and the Kansas City wire asserted that he had been "caught in the very act." No paper gave his race, though the wire singled out only the Chetopa victims as "negroes" and an Iowa editorial counted the week's dead as "three whites and two negroes."

According to a dispatch dated at Minneapolis, a party of forty or fifty masked men from Fountain Township, described as Dorsey's neighbors, entered the town at about 2 a.m. Using a sledge and a bar of railroad iron, they broke open two jail doors, overpowered the jailer "after a lively fight" and made him unlock McCarthy's cell. McCarthy was bound and taken to the Geisen bridge across the Solomon River, about three miles from town, where he was hanged.

Meanwhile the mob's guards stopped the city marshal, kept the sheriff in his room and held townspeople on the streets until the mob left. The Emporia paper called the mob "well organized and heavily armed." At 7 a.m. the sheriff and marshal found the body hanging from the bridge timbers.

The Minneapolis dispatch reported that, while people deprecated "resort to mob law," there was "rather openly expressed sympathy with the action of the mob." No report of an inquest, arrests or prosecution of the mob appears in the coverage. At year's end the Paw Paw True Northerner listed McCarthy among the "Victims of Judge Lynch" for 28 June, beside the two men hanged at Chetopa.

The story first ran on 29 June as part of a Kansas City wire that grouped it with the lynchings of Wallace Mitchell at Syracuse and of John Risbee and Wyley Lee, "negroes," at Chetopa. The New York Sun headlined it "Four Lynchings in Kansas" with the subhead "The Citizens Disgusted by the Law's Leniency Toward Murderers," and explained that no Kansas governor had ever signed a death warrant, calling the day's record "the logical outcome of the situation." Shorter versions of the wire appeared the same day and the next in Washington, Waterbury, St. Paul, Beatrice and Maysville, most calling McCarthy simply "the murderer of Mike Dorsey."

A second, local account dated at Minneapolis, with the Fountain Township details, ran in the Washington Critic on 30 June and in the Emporia Weekly News on 5 July. Headlined "Another Lynching Bee in Kansas," it then circulated through weekly papers in Kentucky, Ohio and Nebraska in early July, while Minnesota and Iowa digests carried one-sentence items.

Editorial comment was divided: the Wheeling Intelligencer wrote that "Lynching is wrong" but that the slowness of justice said to have provoked the lynchings was also to be condemned. An Iowa Citizen editorial reprinted in Abbeville, South Carolina, called the Kansas lynchings "a damnable outrage," while a Burlington Free Press quip, reprinted in Rock Island, joked that Kansas had "lynched four murderers in 24 hours."

The Kansas City wire put the mob at an armed band of 200 riding in at midnight, while the Minneapolis dispatch counted forty or fifty masked men arriving at 2 a.m.; the local dispatch, printed in a Kansas paper, is the closer source. Several short wire items said McCarthy was hanged to a tree, and the Sun used both "tree" and "bridge," but the local account said the body was found hanging from the bridge timbers. The Iowa Citizen editorial alone said two men were lynched at Minneapolis.

accounts.gist: An armed band of 200 rode into town at midnight, posted guards at officials' homes, forced the jailer to give up the keys and hanged McCarthy from the bridge over the 'Soloma River'; the dispatch treated the four Kansas lynchings as the outcome of the state's death-penalty law.

accounts.label: Minneapolis dispatch
accounts.gist: At 2 a.m. forty or fifty masked men from Fountain Township, Dorsey's neighbors, broke in the jail doors, overpowered the jailer, held the marshal, sheriff and townspeople, and hanged McCarthy from the Geisen bridge three miles out; the body was found at 7 a.m.

framing.detail: The Sun's headline said 'The Citizens Disgusted by the Law's Leniency Toward Murderers' and called the day's lynchings 'the logical outcome of the situation' under Kansas law.
Most papers ran short wire or digest items calling McCarthy 'the murderer of Mike Dorsey' under headlines such as 'Four Lynched Within Twenty-four Hours' and 'Another Lynching Bee in Kansas'.
The Kansas account (Emporia) described the jail break plainly and reported local sympathy with the mob alongside deprecation of mob law.
The Wheeling Intelligencer said 'Lynching is wrong' but condemned the slowness of justice said to have provoked it.
An Iowa Citizen editorial reprinted in Abbeville called the Kansas lynchings 'a damnable outrage'.
A Burlington Free Press joke, reprinted in Rock Island, said Kansas did not mean to let New York 'get ahead of them'.
